title: Mozilla/Firefox-MCP
content:
Model Context Protocol server that lets AI agents use Firefox. It has two main use cases:
- Agentic browsing: the agent uses the browser for regular tasks, such as reading pages, filling forms and going through multi-step flows on websites.
- Agent-assisted web development: the agent loads the page you are working on and inspects it with developer tools, such as the console, network requests, the debugger and the profiler.
It controls Firefox through WebDriver BiDi (via Selenium WebDriver) and works with Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Cline and other MCP clients.
Repository: https://github.com/mozilla/firefox-mcp
Also published as @mozilla/firefox-devtools-mcp for existing setups.
Note: This MCP server requires a local Firefox browser installation and cannot run on cloud hosting services like glama.ai. Use npx @mozilla/firefox-mcp@latest to run locally, or use Docker with the provided Dockerfile.
Browser MCP servers carry inherent risks. A few key practices:
- Use a dedicated Firefox profile. Never run the server against your regular profile — the agent has access to whatever the browser can reach, including cookies and saved sessions.
- Be cautious about which sites you visit. Pages can return content designed to manipulate the agent (prompt injection). Stick to sites you control or trust.
- Enable only the tool modules you need. The default basic preset already includes evaluate_script; --tool-preset slim drops it. Higher presets such as --tool-preset developer (debugging, network, console, profiler) and --tool-preset mozilla (privileged context) expand what the agent can do further.
See SECURITY.md for a full breakdown of risks and how to report vulnerabilities.
- Node.js ≥ 20.19.0
- Firefox 100+ installed (auto‑detected, or pass --firefox-path)
Recommended: use npx so you run the latest published version from npm.
claude mcp add firefox npx @mozilla/firefox-mcp@latest
# Headless + viewport via args
claude mcp add firefox npx @mozilla/firefox-mcp@latest -- --headless --viewport 1280x720
# Or via environment variables
claude mcp add firefox npx @mozilla/firefox-mcp@latest \
  --env START_URL=https://example.com \
  --env FIREFOX_HEADLESS=truecodex mcp add firefox -- npx @mozilla/firefox-mcp@latest
# Headless + viewport via args
codex mcp add firefox -- \
  npx @mozilla/firefox-mcp@latest -- --headless --viewport 1280x720
# Or via environment variables
codex mcp add firefox \
  --env START_URL=https://example.com \
  --env FIREFOX_HEADLESS=true \
  -- npx @mozilla/firefox-mcp@latest
Add to Claude Code’s mcp_settings.json:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "firefox": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@mozilla/firefox-mcp@latest", "--headless", "--viewport", "1280x720"],
      "env": {
        "START_URL": "about:blank"
      }
    }
  }
}
Add to ~/.codex/config.toml:
[mcp_servers.firefox]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "@mozilla/firefox-mcp@latest", "--headless", "--viewport", "1280x720"]
[mcp_servers.firefox.env]
START_URL = "about:blank"npm run setup
# Choose Claude Code; the script saves JSON to the right pathnpx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector npx @mozilla/firefox-mcp@latest --start-url https://example.com --headless
Then call tools like:
- list_pages, select_page, navigate_page
- take_snapshot then click_by_uid / fill_by_uid
- list_network_requests (always‑on capture), get_network_request
- list_downloads (always‑on capture), set_download_behavior
- screenshot_page, list_console_messages
You can pass flags or environment variables (names on the right):
- --firefox-path — absolute path to Firefox binary
- --headless — run without UI (FIREFOX_HEADLESS=true)
- --viewport 1280x720 — initial window size
- --profile-path — use a specific Firefox profile. Firefox runs in a firefox_mcp_profile subfolder of that path, marked with a .firefox-mcp file; pointing --profile-path at a marked profile reuses it directly
- --firefox-arg — extra Firefox arguments (repeatable)
- --start-url — open this URL on start (START_URL)
- --accept-insecure-certs — ignore TLS errors (ACCEPT_INSECURE_CERTS=true)
- --connect-existing — attach to an already-running Firefox instead of launching a new one (CONNECT_EXISTING=true)
- --marionette-port — Marionette port for connect-existing mode, default 2828 (MARIONETTE_PORT)
- --idle-timeout — seconds without tool calls after which a connect-existing session releases Firefox, default 1800. Firefox accepts one client at a time, so other clients can only connect once it is released. The next tool call reconnects and selects the tab that is active in Firefox at that moment (IDLE_TIMEOUT)
- --pref name=value — set Firefox preference at startup via moz:firefoxOptions (repeatable)
- --tool-preset — select which tool modules to enable: slim, basic (default), developer, mozilla, or all. See Tool modules and presets. (TOOL_PRESET)
- --tools — explicit list of tool modules to enable, overriding --tool-preset entirely (e.g. --tools pages network script). See Tool modules and presets.
- --enable-script — deprecated, use --tool-preset developer or --tools ... script debugging. Selects the developer tool preset. (ENABLE_SCRIPT=true)
- --enable-privileged-context — deprecated, use --tool-preset mozilla or --tools ... privileged prefs.  Selects the mozilla tool preset. Requires MOZ_REMOTE_ALLOW_SYSTEM_ACCESS=1 (ENABLE_PRIVILEGED_CONTEXT=true)
- --android-device — enable Firefox for Android mode; value is the ADB device serial (e.g. emulator-5554). Run adb devices to list connected devices. Omit the value or use auto to select the single connected device automatically.
- --android-wipe-app-data — confirm that Android mode wipes all data of the target app. Required together with --android-device. (ANDROID_WIPE_APP_DATA=true)
- --android-package — Android app package name, default org.mozilla.firefox. Other packages: org.mozilla.firefox_beta for Firefox Beta, org.mozilla.fenix for Firefox Nightly, org.mozilla.fenix.debug for Firefox Nightly Debug, org.mozilla.geckoview_example for geckoview (ANDROID_PACKAGE)
- --unrestricted-save-paths — let the saveTo parameter write anywhere on disk instead of the default roots. See Saving bulky output to disk and the security note in SECURITY.md. (UNRESTRICTED_SAVE_PATHS=true)
- --log-file — write MCP server logs to a file instead of stderr. Useful for debugging sessions with MCP clients that hide server output. Set DEBUG=* to also include verbose debug logs. Example: --log-file /tmp/firefox-mcp.log
Tools are grouped into modules. You choose which modules to expose either with a named preset
(--tool-preset) or with an explicit list (--tools). When both are given, --tools wins and
the preset is ignored.
Presets (each is a superset of the previous):
- slim — the minimum to browse and interact with pages
- basic (default) — adds tools for regular browsing
- developer — adds tools for web developers
- mozilla — adds tools for Firefox developers
- all — every module
See docs/tools.md for the list of modules and the modules in each preset.
Note that basic, the default, includes script and therefore the evaluate_script tool.
See SECURITY.md for what that means for the attack
surface, and use --tool-preset slim or an explicit --tools list to drop it.
# Use the developer preset (adds network, console, debugging and profiler tools)
npx @mozilla/firefox-mcp --tool-preset developer
# Enable only the modules you need
npx @mozilla/firefox-mcp --tools pages network console
The prefs and privileged modules require MOZ_REMOTE_ALLOW_SYSTEM_ACCESS=1 and are only
available in the Mozilla-internal build. The launch module requires the Mozilla-internal
build too: it restarts Firefox under a caller-chosen binary, profile, environment and set of
preferences, which is a configuration change the operator should own. Use --pref,
--firefox-path and the other command-line options instead. The bidi module also requires
the Mozilla-internal build: it sends any WebDriver BiDi command, so it gives access to what the
other modules expose

report.summary: Mozilla's open-source firefox-mcp lets AI agents drive Firefox via MCP for browsing tasks and web development debugging.
report.background: The Model Context Protocol, introduced by Anthropic in late 2024, standardized how AI assistants call external tools, and browser automation quickly became one of its most used applications. Most early browser MCP servers were built on Chromium via Playwright or Puppeteer, leaving Firefox — and cross-browser testing — underserved. Mozilla has been pushing WebDriver BiDi as the standards-based successor to CDP-only automation, and firefox-mcp is its first-party answer, wrapping Selenium WebDriver and BiDi so clients like Claude Code, Cursor and Cline can control Firefox natively. It also lands as browser vendors compete for agent traffic: Google shipped its own Chrome DevTools MCP, and Microsoft has deep Playwright integrations. Firefox-mcp differentiates by exposing real devtools surface — console, network, debugger, profiler — plus multi-step form and download handling, while keeping everything local for privacy.
key_points: firefox-mcp serves two audiences: agents doing everyday browsing (reading pages, filling forms, completing multi-step site flows) and developers who want an agent to load a local page and inspect it through the console, network panel, debugger or profiler.

It controls Firefox over WebDriver BiDi via Selenium WebDriver, so it inherits a cross-browser standard rather than a proprietary protocol. It supports headless mode, custom viewports, extra Firefox prefs, attaching to an already-running browser, and even Firefox for Android over ADB.

Tool modules are gated behind presets — slim, basic (default), developer, mozilla, all — or an explicit --tools list. Notably, the default basic preset includes evaluate_script, so users who want a smaller attack surface are told to use slim or hand-pick modules.

Mozilla is unusually direct about risk: use a dedicated Firefox profile, never your daily one, since the agent can reach cookies and saved sessions; watch for prompt injection from untrusted pages; and note the server cannot run on cloud hosts because it needs a local Firefox install.

Setup is a one-liner via npx or Docker, with documented integration for Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Cline and Codex, plus a large flag and environment-variable surface for profiles, TLS, idle timeouts and log files.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a signal that browser vendors intend to own the agent-browser interface rather than cede it to third-party Chromium wrappers; Mozilla is betting WebDriver BiDi can compete with CDP by being a standard. For developers, it fills a genuine gap: cross-browser agent testing, real Firefox devtools access, Android support and reproducible local runs without cloud dependency. For regular users, the practical effect is indirect but meaningful — better-tested websites, and agents that can complete real browser tasks on a privacy-respecting engine. The loud security warnings, dedicated-profile guidance and preset system also set a template for how browser MCP servers should handle prompt injection and least privilege, an issue every agentic browsing tool now faces.
report.tools: Try the MCP Inspector (npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector) to poke tools before wiring anything up, and install via npx @mozilla/firefox-mcp@latest or the bundled Dockerfile. @mozilla/firefox-devtools-mcp is the compatibility package for existing setups. Compare against Google's Chrome DevTools MCP and Playwright MCP to see how BiDi and CDP differ in practice, and read the repo's SECURITY.md and docs/tools.md before choosing a preset.
